semantic_correction.stem: A client with a new colostomy looks away during pouch care and says, 'I don't want my partner to see me like this.' Which nursing response is most therapeutic?

options.A: Tell me what worries you most about being seen by your partner. We can discuss ostomy care and support resources that fit your concerns.
options.B: Many people adjust to an ostomy over time. Try not to focus on appearance now; confidence often improves once pouch care becomes routine.
options.C: It may be easier to postpone discussing intimacy until you are independent with pouch care and your physical recovery is further along.
options.D: Your partner may be more accepting than you expect. I can explain the pouching system to both of you so the concern feels less unfamiliar.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI Bookshelf Nursing Skills guidance identifies ostomy-related emotional burden as a legitimate nursing concern that can affect self-esteem, body image, quality of life, and intimacy. It states that nurses can promote healthy coping by arranging appropriate referrals to a wound/ostomy nurse specialist, social worker, or support groups. Current 2025 Open RN therapeutic-communication guidance recommends client-centered, nonjudgmental listening and open-ended questions that encourage expression and build trust. A first invites the client to define the personal concern rather than assuming its meaning, then offers individualized support resources. B is less therapeutic because it redirects the client away from the expressed concern and gives premature reassurance about adjustment. C postpones an important psychosocial issue rather than exploring it now. D assumes how the partner may respond and moves toward teaching before first understanding the client's concern or obtaining the client's preference for partner involvement.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Address ostomy-related body-image and intimacy concerns with open-ended, nonjudgmental, client-centered communication and offer individualized ostomy or psychosocial support resources when desired.
semantic_correction.source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf — Open Resources for Nursing (Open RN)

semantic_correction.source_locator: Nursing Skills Chapter 21, Managing Ostomies → Physical and Emotional Assessment: ostomy emotional burden can affect self-esteem, body image, quality of life, and ability to be intimate; nurses can promote healthy coping through referrals to a wound/ostomy nurse specialist, social worker, and support groups; nurses should monitor their own nonverbal cues. Nursing: Mental Health and Community Concepts Chapter 2 → Therapeutic Communication: therapeutic listening is nonjudgmental; effective therapeutic communication is client-centered, uses active listening, and uses open-ended questions to encourage client expression and build trust; giving advice and dismissive/premature responses are barriers.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI nursing guidance supports direct exploration of ostomy-related body-image and intimacy concerns using client-centered open-ended communication and appropriate referral/support resources rather than avoidance, premature reassurance, or assumptions about the partner.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the uniquely-long correct-answer cue, rebuilt all four responses to nearly identical length, anchored the response directly to current ostomy psychosocial-assessment guidance and 2025 therapeutic-communication guidance, and eliminated assumptions about the client's or partner's adjustment trajectory.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests a therapeutic response to ostomy-related body-image/intimacy concern with one clearly best answer, balanced alternatives, current nursing-text support, and no answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It uses an open-ended, client-centered invitation to explore the concern and then offers individualized ostomy or psychosocial support resources.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. It offers premature reassurance and shifts the client away from discussing the stated body-image/intimacy concern.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. It postpones a legitimate psychosocial concern and implies that discussion must wait for physical or technical recovery.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. It assumes the partner's response and moves to partner teaching before first exploring the client's concern and preference for partner involvement.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone begins with open-ended exploration and preserves client choice; B reassures prematurely, C defers the concern, and D makes an unsupported assumption about the partner before assessing the client's wishes.
cueing_check: All four responses are parallel therapeutic-communication statements of essentially equal length and specificity; the prior uniquely-long correct option was removed and no formatting or absolute-word cue identifies the key.
